name: Advanced chip packaging (OSAT)
one_line: Takes bare chips and turns them into finished packages — bonding, stacking memory beside the processor, and testing. The last mile before a chip can be used.
sells: Assembly, advanced packaging (die stacking and interposer bonding) and final test, done to a customer's chips
customers: Chip designers and foundries (NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom, and the firms whose chips TSMC fabricates)
suppliers: Bare dies and silicon interposers from foundries, HBM stacks, package substrates, and bonding and test equipment

revenue.note: Combined revenue of the top-10 outsourced assembly-and-test firms (TrendForce). One market-research estimate put the broader OSAT market near $52B for 2025; neither figure includes TSMC's in-house advanced packaging (CoWoS), where the AI bottleneck actually sits.

structure.why: ASE alone takes about 45% of outsourced revenue and leads across mainstream and advanced packaging; a handful of rivals split the rest, and the most advanced AI packaging (TSMC's CoWoS) is kept in-house rather than outsourced.
structure.hhi_note: Sum of squared shares of top-10 OSAT revenue (TrendForce, 2024); measured against the whole market it slightly overstates concentration, and it excludes TSMC's in-house advanced packaging.

econ: Complementary inputs and the binding constraint: a working AI accelerator needs both a logic die and the advanced package that bonds high-bandwidth memory beside it, so whichever is scarcer caps total output. Through 2025-26 it has been packaging capacity, not the dies, that limited how many AI chips could ship.
